name: French (Belgium)
family: Indo-European, Romance, Western Romance, Gallo-Romance (langue d'oïl)
variety: French as spoken in Wallonia and Brussels by speakers close to the local standard; stronger regional features (Liège, Hainaut) are noted as such
sources: Fougeron, Cécile and Smith, Caroline L. (1993). French. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 23(2), 73-76. Reprinted in the Handbook of the International Phonetic Association (1999), Cambridge University Press.

Hambye, Philippe and Simon, Anne Catherine (2012). The variation of pronunciation in Belgian French: from segmental phonology to prosody. In Gess, Lyche and Meisenburg (eds.), Phonological Variation in French: Illustrations from Three Continents. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.
Pohl, Jacques (1983). Quelques caractéristiques de la phonologie du français parlé en Belgique. Langue française 60.
Warnant, Léon (1997). Phonétique et phonologie. In Blampain, Goosse, Klinkenberg and Wilmet (eds.), Le français en Belgique. Louvain-la-Neuve: Duculot.
Walter, Henriette (1982). Enquête phonologique et variétés régionales du français. Paris: Presses Universitaires de France.
Simon, Anne Catherine (ed.) (2012). La variation prosodique régionale en français. Bruxelles: De Boeck-Duculot.
Jun, Sun-Ah and Fougeron, Cécile (2002). Realizations of accentual phrase in French intonation. Probus 14, 147-172.
Delais-Roussarie, Elisabeth et al. (2015). Intonational phonology of French: developing a ToBI system for French. In Frota and Prieto (eds.), Intonation in Romance. Oxford University Press.
Calliope (1989). La parole et son traitement automatique. Paris: Masson.
Grabe, Esther and Low, Ee Ling (2002). Durational variability in speech and the rhythm class hypothesis. In Gussenhoven and Warner (eds.), Laboratory Phonology 7. Berlin: Mouton de Gruyter.

vowel_formants.speaker: adult male, reference French of France (means over speakers)
vowel_formants.source: Calliope 1989; no table for Belgian speakers is cited, so these are stand-in values for the oral vowels that Belgian and reference French share

contrasts: four nasal vowels: /ɛ̃/ and /œ̃/ are kept apart (brin versus brun, empreinte versus emprunte), where most speakers in northern France have merged them
the contrast of patte and pâte (tache versus tâche, mal versus mâle) is kept, but as a length contrast [a] versus [aː] rather than by a back vowel quality
/ɛ/ versus long /ɛː/ (mettre versus maître, faite versus fête, bette versus bête, lettre versus l'être)

vowel length at the end of a word: a final vowel followed by written e is long (ami [ami] versus amie [amiː], bout versus boue, nu versus nue, armé versus armée), so many masculine and feminine forms differ
/e/ versus /ɛ/ in final open syllables (piqué versus piquais, né versus naît, future -ai versus conditional -ais)
/o/ versus /ɔ/ and /ø/ versus /œ/ in closed syllables (côte versus cote, jeûne versus jeune)
the usual French consonant contrasts, with /ɥ/ absent or marginal for many speakers
allophony: /ɥ/ is replaced by [w] before /i/ (huit [wit], lui [lwi], puis [pwi], nuit [nwi]) and by the vowel [y] in hiatus elsewhere (tuer [ty.e], nuage [ny.aʒ])
high vowels before another vowel often stay syllabic, with a glide in between, where reference French has a glide: lion [li.jɔ̃], lier [li.je], louer [lu.e], nouer

word-final voiced obstruents are devoiced by many speakers, above all in the east (Liège), while the preceding vowel stays long: grande [ɡʁɑ̃ːt], rouge [ʁuːʃ], neige [nɛːʃ]; the feature is regional and stigmatised
vowels are long before final /ʁ z ʒ v/ as in reference French, and the long vowels of the dialect are clearly longer than in France
long final vowels may end in a glide in Wallonia: amie [amiːj], année [aneːj]
written w is [w] in wagon, Wallonie and similar words, where France has [v]
/ʁ/ is a uvular fricative, voiceless next to voiceless consonants
phonotactics: schwa can be dropped when the resulting cluster is allowed, as in reference French
liaison and enchaînement link a final consonant to a following vowel
word-final obstruent plus liquid clusters (quatre, table) are simplified in everyday speech

stress.rule: The last full syllable of each accentual phrase is prominent; an optional early rise can mark the start of the phrase; some regional accents add prominence or length on the penultimate syllable.
stress.cues: lengthening of the final syllable and a pitch movement on it; intensity plays little part

rhythm.vowel_reduction: none in quality; schwa can be dropped
rhythm.notes: The contrastive long vowels add durational variability compared with reference French. The nPVI figure is for a speaker from France and is given for orientation only.

npvi_v.source: Grabe and Low 2002 (one speaker of French from France, not Belgian French)

length.notes: Length is contrastive for final vowels (amie, boue, nue, armée), for /ɛ/ versus /ɛː/ and for /a/ versus /aː/. No duration ratio is cited here.

intonation.declarative: a rise on the last syllable of each non-final accentual phrase, optional early rise at the start of a phrase, and a fall to low on the last syllable of the utterance
intonation.yes_no_question: with statement word order, a rise on the last syllable to a high boundary; with est-ce que or inversion the rise is smaller or the contour falls
intonation.wh_question: high on the question word, then a fall to a low ending; a final rise is also possible
intonation.continuation: rise on the last syllable of the phrase, larger at major boundaries
intonation.accent_shape: LH* on the last full syllable of the accentual phrase, with an optional initial rise LHi near its start
intonation.notes: The phonological system is that of French in general (Jun and Fougeron 2002; Delais-Roussarie et al. 2015). Studies in Simon (2012) report regional differences, among them lengthening of the penultimate syllable in some Walloon accents.

problems: the voice is the voice of France with other number words: the only conditional entries for Belgium are septante and nonante in the word list; phonemes, rules and tunes are shared
brin and brun get different phoneme names (E~ and W~, printed [ɛ̃] and [œ̃]), but both phonemes play the same vowel data (vnasal/W_n) with the same length, so the contrast cannot be heard
no long /ɛː/: mettre and maître, faite and fête, bette and bête are identical
no length in final vowels: ami and amie, bout and boue, nu and nue, armé and armée are identical
/ɥ/ is a short [y] before i (huit [yˈit], lui [lyˈi]); the Belgian [w] is not available, nor the syllabic high vowels of lion, louer (lier [ljˈe], louer [lwˈe])
rose and chose have open [ɔ] ([ʁˈɔz], [ʃˈɔz]) where Belgian French has long close [oː]
jeune is given the close vowel [ø], so jeune and jeûne differ only by length; the contrast is [œ] versus [øː]
devoicing of final voiced obstruents and penultimate lengthening are not available as options
good: 70 and 90 are read septante and nonante, and 80 quatre-vingts, as in Belgium
patte and pâte, tache and tâche, mal and mâle differ by length ([a] against [aː]), which is how Belgian French keeps this contrast
/e/ and /ɛ/ are kept apart in final syllables (piqué against piquais, né against naît)
côte [koːt] and cote [kɔt] differ; prominence is phrase-final and the French tune set is used

notes: Belgian French keeps a vowel system that is more conservative than that of Paris: four nasal vowels and distinctive length. A voice for it needs a separate nasal vowel for brun, long vowels in the rules (final e after a vowel, ê, aî) and the [w] of huit.
